## [NVIDIA Releases TensorRT Model Connect in Public Preview: Hugging Face Checkpoint to Native C++ Inference in Two Commands](https://www.marktechpost.com/2026/08/18/nvidia-releases-tensorrt-model-connect-in-public-preview-hugging-face-checkpoint-to-native-c-inference-in-two-commands/)
*MarkTechPost* | 18/08/2026 | Score: 0.80
Tags: research_paper, model_release, inference, hardware, open_source

> NVIDIA has released TensorRT Model Connect (TRTMC) in public preview, an Apache-2.0 project that takes a supported Hugging Face or local checkpoint to end-to-end TensorRT inference in two commands, with no intermediate ONNX export. The build emits a versioned .bundle artifact that runs through native C++ task APIs, so inference executes without PyTorch in the runtime path. NVIDIA's July 29, 2026 GB300 snapshot covers 105 release profiles across 76 model families. The post NVIDIA Releases TensorRT Model Connect in Public Preview: Hugging Face Checkpoint to Native C++ Inference in Two Commands appeared first on MarkTechPost .

## [Auditing Preference Biases and Fine-Tuning Language Models with Direct Preference Optimization on Anthropic HH-RLHF Using TRL and LoRA](https://www.marktechpost.com/2026/08/20/auditing-preference-biases-and-fine-tuning-language-models-with-direct-preference-optimization-on-anthropic-hh-rlhf-using-trl-and-lora/)
*MarkTechPost* | 20/08/2026 | Score: 0.80
Tags: research_paper, evaluation, dataset, training

> This tutorial provides an end-to-end workflow for fine-tuning language models using Direct Preference Optimization (DPO). We demonstrate how to audit the Anthropic HH-RLHF dataset for structural and length-based biases, implement a robust training pipeline using TRL and LoRA, and evaluate model performance to ensure genuine preference learning rather than reliance on lexical shortcuts. The post Auditing Preference Biases and Fine-Tuning Language Models with Direct Preference Optimization on Anthropic HH-RLHF Using TRL and LoRA appeared first on MarkTechPost .

## [Mojo🔥 is now open source](https://simonwillison.net/2026/Aug/18/mojo-is-now-open-source/)
*Simon Willison's Blog* | 18/08/2026 | Score: 0.72
Tags: model_release, hardware, open_source

> <p><strong><a href="https://www.modular.com/blog/mojo-open-source">Mojo🔥 is now open source</a></strong></p> The Mojo programming language has been promising an open source release <a href="https://simonwillison.net/2023/May/4/mojo/">since May 2023</a>. Last week they <a href="https://www.modular.com/blog/modular-26-5-mojo-1-0-is-here">shipped their 1.0</a> and today they have followed through on that original promise, releasing the compiler and toolchain under an Apache 2 license.</p> <p>When Mojo first launched the stated goal was to produce a superset of Python, so existing Python code could be used to bootstrap their own ecosystem. That plan changed <a href="https://forum.modular.com/t/mojo-vision-document-and-roadmap/2187">around August 2025</a>:</p> <blockquote> <p>Mojo may or may not evolve into a full superset of Python, and it’s okay if it doesn’t.</p> <p>We’re encouraged by how well AI-assisted coding tools already help migrate Python to Mojo today, and we’re confident that future tooling and ecosystem maturity will make this evolution even smoother.</p> </blockquote> <p>Today Mojo is its own language, optimized to make GPU programming as painless as possible using syntax inspired by Python, if not 100% compatible with existing code. <p><small></small>Via <a href="https://lobste.rs/s/01lxuf/mojo_is_now_open_source">Lobste.rs</a></small></p> <p>Tags: <a href="https://simonwillison.net/tags/open-source">open-source</a>, <a href="https://simonwillison.net/tags/python">python</a>, <a href="https://simonwillison.net/tags/mojo">mojo</a></p>

## [pnpm 12 RC 8](https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/releases/tag/v12.0.0-rc.8)
*GitHub Releases · pnpm* | 20/08/2026 | Score: 0.70
Tags: model_release, evaluation, api_update

> <h2>Minor Changes</h2> <ul> <li> <p><code>packageImportMethod: auto</code> now tries hardlinks before cloning on Linux. A reflink materializes a new inode and copies extent bookkeeping inside the filesystem's metadata trees, where a hardlink is one directory entry — on btrfs this roughly halves the time an install spends materializing <code>node_modules</code> from a warm store. ext4 installs are unchanged (cloning was never supported there, so <code>auto</code> already hardlinked), and macOS keeps clone-first, where APFS <code>clonefile</code> is the platform's cheap primitive. Cloning remains the fallback when the store refuses hardlinks, and remains available explicitly via <code>packageImportMethod: clone</code>.</p> <p>This ships with pnpm 12 only: pnpm 11's importer deliberately keeps clone-first, since changing what the default materializes on disk is not a point-release change.</p> </li> </ul> <h2>Patch Changes</h2> <ul> <li> <p><code>pnpm approve-builds</code> now removes <code>onlyBuiltDependencies</code>, <code>onlyBuiltDependenciesFile</code>, <code>neverBuiltDependencies</code>, and <code>ignoredBuiltDependencies</code> from <code>pnpm-workspace.yaml</code> when it writes <code>allowBuilds</code>. Those settings were replaced by <code>allowBuilds</code> in pnpm 11 and silently ignored since, so a workspace migrated from pnpm 10 kept them around looking active.</p> </li> <li> <p><code>pnpm audit</code> no longer reports a patched version that was never published or is deprecated. The inferred patched range (e.g. <code>>=4.17.24</code> from <code><=4.17.23</code>) is now checked against the registry packument, and the report is corrected to the lowest non-deprecated published version that satisfies it (e.g. <code>>=4.18.1</code> when <code>4.17.24</code> does not exist and <code>4.18.0</code> is deprecated). When no published version satisfies the range, the report shows <code>Patched versions: None</code>. This also prevents <code>pnpm audit --fix</code> from adding overrides or <code>minimumReleaseAgeExclude</code> entries for patches that do not exist <a href="https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13824" data-hovercard-type="issue" data-hovercard-url="/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13824/hovercard">#13824</a>.</p> <p><code>pnpm audit --fix</code> and <code>pnpm audit --fix update</code> no longer add a <code>minimumReleaseAgeExclude</code> entry when the registry packument shows that the minimum patched version was never published. Previously such entries were written for versions that do not exist, which would have let a later publish of that version bypass the <code>minimumReleaseAge</code> gate <a href="https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/issues/11563" data-hovercard-type="issue" data-hovercard-url="/pnpm/pnpm/issues/11563/hovercard">#11563</a>.</p> <p>The <code>--json</code> output of <code>pnpm audit</code> now returns <code>patched_versions: null</code> for advisories whose inferred patch is not available (never published, skipped, yanked, or deprecated), making it easier for tooling to distinguish "no fix available" from "fix available at version X".</p> </li> <li> <p>Re-fetch full registry metadata when <code>minimumReleaseAge</code> is enabled and an abbreviated packument's <code>time</code> map omits timestamps for some versions. This prevents mature versions from being filtered out and resolution from falling back to the lowest matching version <a href="https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13741" data-hovercard-type="issue" data-hovercard-url="/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13741/hovercard">pnpm/pnpm#13741</a>.</p> </li> <li> <p>A config dependency carrying an inline integrity (the <code><version>+<integrity></code> form, or the object form without a <code>tarball</code>) now takes its tarball URL from the registry's packument instead of deriving it from the registry URL, so migrating one costs an extra metadata request. On a registry that serves tarballs from a path pnpm cannot derive, GitLab's group endpoint for one, installing such a config dependency failed with a 404 while the same package installed fine as a regular dependency <a href="https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13765" data-hovercard-type="issue" data-hovercard-url="/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13765/hovercard">#13765</a>.</p> </li> <li> <p>Don't treat files like <code>license16.json</code> as a package license when deciding if the workspace LICENSE file should be included in the packed package.</p> </li> <li> <p>Reduced warm update overhead by limiting virtual-store bin linking and ignored-script build bookkeeping to packages materialized by the current install.</p> </li> <li> <p><code>pnpm init</code> now pins the exact pnpm version instead of a <code>^</code> range, and records it in the <code>packageManager</code> field alongside <code>devEngines.packageManager</code>. Corepack reads only <code>packageManager</code> and accepts nothing but an exact version, so it rejected the generated <code>package.json</code> with "expected a semver version" <a href="https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13969" data-hovercard-type="issue" data-hovercard-url="/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13969/hovercard">pnpm/pnpm#13969</a>. A package created inside an existing workspace is still left unpinned — it follows the pin at the workspace root — and <code>--no-init-package-manager</code> still scaffolds a manifest without any pin. In pnpm 12, <code>pnpm init</code> also honors <code>initType</code> and its <code>--init-type</code> flag, so the manifest it writes is the same one pnpm 11 writes.</p> </li> <li> <p><code>node-linker=hoisted</code> installs no longer produce broken layouts on graphs with version conflicts. Three hoister fixes, aligning with <code>@yarnpkg/nm</code> (which the TypeScript CLI delegates to):</p> <ul> <li>A version-conflicted package depended on by several packages kept its conflicting transitive dependencies under only one of the dependents, so requiring them through any other dependent resolved the wrong (root-hoisted) version — for example an ESM <code>parse-entities@4</code> resolving <code>character-entities-legacy</code> v1 instead of v3, which crashes with <code>ERR_IMPORT_ATTRIBUTE_MISSING</code> on Node.js 22. Hoist decisions are now made per parent path on decoupled copies (ports upstream's <code>decoupleGraphNode</code>).</li> <li>Peer-resolution variants of one package version now collapse onto a single copy (ports pnpm v11's <code>depPathByPkgId</code> mapping) instead of conflict-nesting a copy under every dependent — on peer-variant-heavy graphs (such as <code>bit</code>'s) the old behavior also made the per-path walk explode.</li> <li>Hoisting no longer shadows names a subtree resolves through an ancestor directory: a candidate is refused when a nearer ancestor holds a different version of its name (upstream's "filled by parent" scan) or when the hoist root's subtree already resolves that name from above (upstream's <code>usedDependencies</code> gate).</li> </ul> </li> <li> <p><code>pnpm update --no-save <pkg>@<version></code> now keeps the manifest's declared importer specifier in <code>pnpm-lock.yaml</code> when the requested version satisfies that range, so a subsequent <code>--frozen-lockfile</code> install no longer fails because the lockfile records the requested version as the specifier.</p> </li> <li> <p>Reduced registry metadata requests during dependency resolution by reusing cached metadata when lockfile preferences prove that no uncached version can win <a href="https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13976" data-hovercard-type="issue" data-hovercard-url="/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13976/hovercard">pnpm/pnpm#13976</a>.</p> </li> <li> <p>Improved install performance: the store-index writer's shutdown now overlaps the install's final lockfile and <code>.modules.yaml</code> writes instead of extending the install's tail.</p> </li> <li> <p>A setting in the global <code>config.yaml</code> that pnpm does not read from that file, or that is written in kebab-case instead of camelCase, is now reported instead of being ignored silently.</p> </li> <li> <p>A forced full re-resolution (config changes the fast lockfile update cannot absorb, such as a changed override or <code>packageExtensions</code>) no longer moves dependencies whose recorded versions still satisfy their ranges. The prior lockfile now pins each still-satisfied edge even when its recorded subtree cannot be reused wholesale, so open ranges like <code>@types/node: "*"</code> keep their locked versions instead of collapsing onto the highest locked version and churning the lockfile.</p> </li> <li> <p>Improved fresh resolution performance when package metadata is already cached.</p> </li> <li> <p>Improved fresh installs by reusing the store index and verified-files cache during dependency materialization.</p> </li> <li> <p>A runtime installed through <code>devEngines.runtime</code> now matches the host when <code>supportedArchitectures</code> lists several platforms. Listing <code>os: [darwin, linux]</code> and <code>cpu: [x64, arm64]</code> used to install the runtime built for the first entry of each list, so a machine running Linux on arm64 got a macOS x64 Node.js that could not execute <a href="https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13898" data-hovercard-type="issue" data-hovercard-url="/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13898/hovercard">#13898</a>.</p> </li> <li> <p><code>pnpm self-update <tag></code> no longer downgrades when the dist-tag points at the pnpm version already running and that version is younger than <code>minimumReleaseAge</code>. The maturity cutoff moved the tag back to the previous mature release, so <code>pnpm self-update next-12</code> on v12.0.0-rc.4 switched to v12.0.0-rc.3.</p> </li> <li> <p>Improved install performance: large tarballs are now verified and extracted while they download, so the biggest packages — whose downloads finish last — no longer add their whole extraction to the end of the install.</p> </li> </ul>

The Python <code>EmbeddingModel.embed()</code>, <code>EmbeddingModel.embed_multi()</code>, <code>Collection.embed()</code> and <code>Collection.embed_multi()</code> methods accept <code>key=</code> too, passing the resolved per-call key to embedding plugins without changing shared model state. Existing plugins that read <code>self.key</code> continue to work through a compatibility fallback. Thanks, <a href="https://github.com/ChrisJr404">ChrisJr404</a>. <a href="https://github.com/simonw/llm/issues/757">#757</a>, <a href="https://github.com/simonw/llm/pull/1620">#1620</a></li> </ul> </blockquote> <p>The embedding models now use the same pattern for keys that regular LLM models do.</p> <blockquote> <ul> <li><code>llm prompt -t/--template</code> can now be repeated to combine templates in order. This allows model configuration and options from one template to be used with a prompt from another.</li> </ul> </blockquote> <p>This unlocks a neat pattern where you can create templates that package a model with a set of default options:</p> <pre><code>llm -m gpt-5.6-luna -o reasoning_effort high --save lhigh llm "Generate an SVG of a pelican riding a bicycle" --save pelican # Combine and run the templates llm -t lhigh -t pelican </code></pre> <blockquote> <ul> <li>Reasoning-capable Responses API models now support a <code>reasoning_summary</code> option with <code>auto</code>, <code>concise</code>, and <code>detailed</code> values. This can be used with <a href="https://llm.datasette.io/en/stable/other-models.html#openai-endpoint">llm openai endpoint --responses</a>. <a href="https://github.com/simonw/llm/issues/1600">#1600</a></li> </ul> </blockquote> <p>This is particularly useful for exercising different models that provide their own imitation of the OpenAI Responses API.</p> <p>Tags: <a href="https://simonwillison.net/tags/annotated-release-notes">annotated-release-notes</a>, <a href="https://simonwillison.net/tags/llm">llm</a></p>

## [5 Things I Learned About People From Doing Stand-Up Comedy](https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/3CdKcgo8vrb2hxEFd/5-things-i-learned-about-people-from-doing-stand-up-comedy-1)
*LessWrong* | 22/08/2026 | Score: 0.80
Tags: research_paper, architecture

> (People had complained about me just posting a preview of the linked post, so here's the whole thing!) I’ve been doing stand-up comedy for two months now, which is a total gear shift from my previous job in AI policy. I’ve learned some fascinating things about how humor works, but also about how people perceive each other, and how crowds can be surprisingly hive-minded. For those interested in improving their models of people and the world, here are five of those things! 1. People need to put you in a box The first thing a stand-up audience craves, consciously or unconsciously, is for you to tell them what kind of person you are. Are you an artsy lesbian, a hard-working immigrant, a married average Joe? For some reason, people can’t laugh until they have a box to put you in. If they can’t place a comedian, half the audience’s minds will be occupied trying to figure out who is talking to them. Must be some sort of innate human drive to quickly categorize new people you meet. This is why so many stand-ups start by addressing their appearance, accent, etc. (“I know what you’re thinking… [generic punchline about their appearance].”) I experienced this need to categorize myself when watching&nbsp; this set by Robby Hoffman &nbsp;recently. I couldn’t quite figure out who was speaking to me and just felt like I couldn’t quite settle until I got more of a grasp on who she is as a person. (This is less applicable to comedians who don’t tell stories or talk conversationally, and instead purely do one-liners. This style of comedy can feel less personal, so I suppose that’s why the urge to know more about the comedian may be lower.) In comedy, something glaring in the audience’s mind that goes unaddressed is called a “loop”. Common loops are a strange/loud laugh in the crowd, something going wrong on stage, or mentioning something that makes the audience concerned, such as the death of a relative. Generally, comedians want to “close” such loops as quickly as possible because people just can’t laugh while thinking “She just knocked over the microphone and hasn’t addressed it!” or “Is he okay?” Some comedians go as far as to address their appearance/voice/etc. every time. Helen Bauer says she has to address being fat every time she goes on stage because there are some people in the audience to whom apparently this poses a loop. Some people’s loops are dumb. I think people’s need to categorize comedians as soon as they get on stage is basically a kind of loop. And I think the fact that people do this to comedians is indicative of people doing this in everyday life too. 2. Laughter is very un-individual I had NO idea how un-independent people’s impulse to laugh is of the people surrounding them until I got into comedy. You will get flat responses, awkward silences, crickets one day and then roaring laughter the next&nbsp; with the exact same set . And it’s not a case of a few people laughing the first day while most stay silent, and the reverse the next day. People’s laughter is pretty even on a given day; people&nbsp; adjust&nbsp; to the energy in the room. (What determines the level of energy in a room, other than the quality of the stand-up set? Probably some combination of the energy level right before the set and the presence of a couple of nutters who unconsciously&nbsp; do not &nbsp;gauge whether and how loud other people are laughing before laughing themselves. Yay, thank you, nutters.) The thing is, most of us do not listen to a joke, evaluate it on its own terms, and decide to laugh. Instead, we are extremely sensitive to how much other people around us are laughing. If the energy is flat, we too are flat. The crazy thing is we don’t&nbsp; choose &nbsp;to laugh more or less. We simply find it more or less funny. The same person could have a completely different experience at a show, depending on the night they choose to go. And they would never know! 3. Different countries’ audiences differ I suppose many people would expect different countries to have different affinities for stand-up—polite laughter in Britain, raucous crowds in Latin America, frigid Germans. I’m generally quite skeptical of such country stereotyping. But for stand-up audiences, it’s true. I can speak best to the difference between British and German audiences since I’m German—it’s huge. You could watch the funniest German stand-up clip you have ever seen on Youtube, and the audience will be giving nothing. ( Little treat if you speak German. ) Stand-up isn’t big in Germany at all; people aren’t that into it. British audiences are super nice in comparison! The strange thing is, I&nbsp; totally get &nbsp;why Germans are like that.&nbsp; I would be like that &nbsp;if I hadn’t moved to the UK years ago. It’s a cultural difference in how you interact with strangers. Germans don’t talk to random people in queues or at bars, etc., in the same way that British people do. Germans don’t cheer easily or join in some sort of audience/crowdwork interaction. To a German, being that outgoing can seem fake and tacky, not to mention exhausting. (It can feel like Brits have a bit more goodwill towards their fellow woman, and honestly, having lived here for a while, maybe Germans could use more of that!) I hear that Belgian audiences are similarly tough, and I imagine the Nordics might be even worse (or maybe that’s just my stereotypes). Reputedly, black audiences also differ from mainly-white ones, but I can’t speak to that difference myself. 4. There’s no single way to work From my background in AI policy, I’m used to there being quite a clear model image for how to become successful in a given line of work. You want to be a researcher? Get yourself a good supervisor, produce a lot of papers, and network. Want to work in policy? Move to London (or DC), go to a million happy hours, and learn to squeeze yourself into really short attention spans. Most importantly, work a 9-7 workday Monday to Friday, or ideally, Monday to Sunday. I’m sort of shocked at how there seems to be absolutely no theme to how successful stand-up comedians work. Not only is no one doing 9-5s, they don’t even agree on what writing looks like at a very basic level. Some comedians sit down with a pen and paper in an office, others compose lines in their head as they go about their day (wtf, how?), and finally, some nutcases&nbsp; go on stage &nbsp;with nothing more than an idea and just figure it out (??). Much in contrast to the ethos in the professional worlds I know, there just doesn’t seem to be an agreed-upon model way to become successful. To give some examples,&nbsp; Nate Bargatze , one of the most successful US comedians, apparently never sits down with pen and paper. Instead, he composes his sets entirely in his head, without even writing them down. (He said this on&nbsp; an episode of the Good One podcast , if I remember correctly.) Judy Carter, author of the “Comedy Bible”, recommends ranting out loud about a topic to find jokes, which doesn’t click for me at all but works for many people. Many experienced comedians go on stage with little more than an idea and just riff (e.g.&nbsp; James Acaster &nbsp;does this). This is sometimes called “writing on stage”. Some comedians like Chris Rock have word-for-word scripts and choreograph their act down to the raise of an eyebrow.&nbsp; Maria Bamford &nbsp;practices her sets standing directly in front of a mirror. Others have the key notes in their head and fill in the rest. My general sense regarding work ethic is that UK and Australian comedians are a bit laissez-faire about it. At the same time, comedians in New York (the stand-up capital of the US) will often do 2-3 shows&nbsp; a night . The most “sensible” comedian I know of is probably Jimmy Carr, who treats it like a 9-5 job (though surely complicated a lot by touring etc.) I suppose what we call stand-up comedy is really a blanket term for quite a range of formats and styles. It encompasses storytelling, crowdwork and some improv, tightly scripted one-liners, characters, clowning, etc. It makes sense that the “process” differs for these. Stand-up writing is also such a personal thing, unlike, e.g., writing a research paper, so again it makes sense that the process is quite personal. The only agreed-upon parts of the success formula are, as far as I can tell, get as much stage time as possible, and be nice. Received wisdom is that doing a lot of gigs makes you better (though it’s a bit unclear to me how that trades off against writing time) and that assholes don’t get booked. You also hear many stories about people regretting not being nicer to the random MC who went on to produce [insert famous TV show here]. 5. People have different senses of humor Duh. But still, I did not fully appreciate this until I got into stand-up. People will be doubling over at sets of one-liners that will leave me absolutely cold. I don’t have much of an appreciation for clever construction of “joke” jokes, apparently. On the other hand, I will be in tears watching&nbsp; Sam Campbell get a hall full of people to bow to images of apes , while other people are simply confused. I’m often completely unable to tell whether a stand-up set is good or not, because it’s just not my sense of humor; it’s not&nbsp; for me . (E.g. I know&nbsp; Maria Bamford &nbsp;is the GOAT, but I will never understand why.) Amy Matthews articulated it something like this&nbsp; on the Always Be Comedy podcast : We don’t have the same cultural fluency about different genres and tastes of comedy that we do with music or movies. If you’re not into heavy metal, you wouldn’t go to a heavy metal concert and then conclude “these musicians are shit”. But it is quite common for people to conclude “this comedian is shit” when the comedian is simply not their sense of humor. We don’t even have good names for different senses of humor, which goes to show how underappreciated these divisions in taste are. This is all just to say, if you ever see&nbsp; me &nbsp;do a set, please resist the urge (you’ll no doubt feel) to shout “You’re shit!”, and instead shout “You’re amazing at a style of comedy that just isn’t my cup of tea!” Thank you. If you liked this post, please check out my substack ! Discuss

## [14 High-Impact Projects for Ambitious Students](https://forum.effectivealtruism.org/posts/hZxjcpCLQ6YdRdHRh/14-high-impact-projects-for-ambitious-students)
*Effective Altruism Forum* | 21/08/2026 | Score: 0.80
Tags: research_paper, model_release

> Published on August 21, 2026 7:54 PM GMT Note: In my view, one of the most impactful opportunities for university students is running a great club for an important cause. E.g, a student group focused on Effective Altruism, AI Safety, Moral Ambition, Animal Welfare, Global Development, improving policy or politics, or other important causes.&nbsp; This document lists ideas other than organizing a high-impact student club (potentially for students at schools that already have strong-performing clubs, or students curious to explore other impactful projects). For more information on starting an impactful EA student group, you can check out this post collating resources for making university organizing fun and easy. Onto the projects! 1) Setting up institutions related to EA or impactful causes at your university. This might involve&nbsp;presenting an idea like&nbsp; NYU’s Center for Mind, Ethics, and Policy ,&nbsp; Stanford Existential Risk Initiative , or the&nbsp; Stanford Alt Protein Project to a relevant department at your university. Then, securing professor backing to mentor student researchers through a university institute over the summer. Then, applying for university funding to support research and other work to advance the mission of the institute and create impact in the world.&nbsp; 2) Writing op-eds for the student newspaper (many of which have high student/alumni readership), to raise awareness about doing good effectively in a non-controversial way. Examples include&nbsp; this piece on effective giving , and lots ( 1 ,&nbsp; 2 ,&nbsp; 3 ,&nbsp; 4 ) of coverage on Harvard’s School For Moral Ambition society!&nbsp; 3) Reaching out to your university about a student-taught, for-credit class related to doing good effectively. This could be particularly impactful if your school’s policy on for-credit student classes is flexible. E.g, Wesleyan University's&nbsp; Student Forums . 4) Advocating (alongside other students) for your university to feature a impactful book as their summer pre-read for incoming freshmen. Examples include the 80,000 Hours Career Guide , Doing Good Better , Moral Ambition , or The Life You Can Save .&nbsp; 5) Owning logistics for regional EA retreats: Last spring, a number of EA university groups in the northeast spent a weekend together learning about doing good. The cost was modest (under $200 per person for the weekend), and the retreat provided an opportunity for students to spend more time engaging with EA ideas than they might spend in a whole semester of weekly meetings through their university group. This retreat didn’t happen the prior year, and likely wouldn’t have happened this year had it not been for an incredibly dedicated student organizer (who didn’t even go to a school in the northeast)! There is a real need for capacity in managing logistics for retreats like this (e.g., finding an affordable venue, creating a notion page, inviting guest speakers etc.) If you might be interested in helping make logistics for regional retreats happen, 10-30 hours of volunteering can make a huge difference. Please email me at sa9156[at]princeton.edu if you’re interested in getting involved! 6) Leveraging university branding to generate interest in doing good! This can include: Hosting virtual programs as an extension of your university EA club that are welcoming to both university students and non-students (e.g, an EA intro fellowship, giving games, cause specific programs like an animal welfare fellowship, etc).&nbsp; As an example, Stanford EA launched a publicly-accessible virtual program during Covid, which got hundreds of participants and turned into&nbsp; EA virtual programs !&nbsp; Producing and sharing club-recommended career and giving opportunities. Using book launches to host and promote speaking engagements on campus.&nbsp; 7) Supporting classmates in applying for&nbsp; university funding to volunteer with impactful nonprofits (e.g, global development organizations that may not have funding to offer paid internships).&nbsp; 8) Joining the&nbsp; EA Anywhere Slack and posting about how you may be able to help others in the introductions channel. Examples could include: “I live in X city and I’m excited to commit Y hours per week to helping with in-person events, or scouting office spaces/retreat venues for organizations, etc. Please reach out if your org could use support!” “I have experience with X skill which I think high-impact orgs could benefit from. I’d love to help your org. ”&nbsp; Example skills could range from copyediting, improving social media strategy, negotiation, AI enablement and infosecurity, paralegal work, government relations, submitting successful grant applications to foundations outside the EA movement, etc. “I’d love to hear what pain points your org has: I’ll be happy to spend some time researching what solutions other orgs have found.” 9) Creating Career newsletters tailored towards new audiences.&nbsp; E.g, I put together a newsletter about impactful careers for policy masters students, largely drawing on EA job boards and the EA DC newsletter. Student interest has been high (less than 5% of joiners end up unsubscribing, open and clickthrough rates are promising), and I think it would be interesting to spread impactful career resources to other groups doing good. This could look like: Replicating this for other masters programs (e.g. Public Health, Sustainability, Divinity, Social Work); reaching out to current students to share a signup form with peers in their program, then sending a monthly newsletter (which itself links to other career infrastructure like Probably Good, 80k, etc.) Asking university career service centers if they’re willing to feature career resources you send on their online career portals. Looking into&nbsp; acquiring social impact newsletters . 10). If you have personal connections to large platforms, helping thought leaders share messaging about effective giving and careers with new audiences. This could look like: TV and film contacts interested in helping EA continue to tell its story (e.g.,&nbsp; Zorilla ,&nbsp; Kokotajlo ,&nbsp; Wildeford ,&nbsp; MacAskill ) Conferences or podcasts (e.g.,&nbsp; Bollard ,&nbsp; Boeree ,&nbsp; MacAskill ) Faith ,&nbsp; university , or&nbsp; corporate event platforms that can host book tours or presentations 11) Proposing and leading impactful volunteering projects with existing service groups.&nbsp; If your city, university, or employer organizes volunteering projects, leading a high-impact project could leverage a large group’s efforts. For example, the EA Foundation organized a volunteer advocacy drive in support of foreign aid that led the city of Zurich to contribute&nbsp; millions of dollars toward development assistance . It could be worth reaching out to your local Rotary International chapter to see if they may be excited in supporting similar international development efforts. I could also imagine you might find traction by arranging impactful volunteer events for university clubs. In my experience, service-oriented club participants often enjoy social activities that help them make friends by spending a weekend on a cause they care about. This could look like door-knocking/phone banking for impactful political change within a civic activism club, or coordinating group conference volunteering at AVA or Sentient Futures with your school’s plant-based club. 12) Exploring neglected effective fundraising channels, for example: Setting up fundraising events in affluent areas for effective nonprofits. This may be particularly lucrative if the nonprofits have broad appeal like GiveWell, Project Resource Optimization, Giving Green, or an effective charity based near the community (e.g. CA Yimby, Open New York, etc.) Speaking with Corporate Social Responsibility staff to facilitate high-impact&nbsp; corporate philanthropy . 13) Working on a socially impactful research project (potentially even for academic credit!) Below are Effective Thesis ' research topic archives (they also offer fellowships, workshops, mentorship and internships for students pursuing impactful research): Expansive Database Global Health&nbsp; Animal welfare AI safety Biosecurity Other research opportunities include building a living literature review for an important cause (example:&nbsp; Lauren Gilbert on Migration ), or identifying areas that don’t have significant EA funding yet but seem like strong candidates for funding (example: Coefficient Giving’s&nbsp; cause exploration prize . 14). Finding projects (volunteer or paid) on the&nbsp; EA Opportunities Board , or&nbsp; Hive !&nbsp; Finally,&nbsp; here is a Claude-compiled list of links to others’ project ideas.&nbsp; Discuss

## [Building a Campus EA Group in No Time (Resources for Students!)](https://forum.effectivealtruism.org/posts/g6jw3PBvPueY2J6ZQ/building-a-campus-ea-group-in-no-time-resources-for-students)
*Effective Altruism Forum* | 21/08/2026 | Score: 0.80
Tags: research_paper, inference

> Published on August 21, 2026 7:18 PM GMT In my view, starting or growing university EA groups is one of the best opportunities to do good while in school. As a grad student working part time at Coefficient Giving, I believe that (per hour) time spent building our EA Group has been similarly impactful to grantmaking work. I’m proud to have been part of the organizing team which revitalized Princeton’s EA group into an active community, with a dozen members spending their summers at high-impact orgs and 150 students involved in our 8-week summer learning program.&nbsp; I suspect there are a number of students who are interested in EA but already have other commitments and feel overwhelmed by the prospect of growing a club alone. [1] &nbsp;If you can relate, I’m glad you’re reading this.&nbsp; I hope this post conveys that important university organizing work can be manageable and fun for busy students. I think community building can even support one’s own career opportunities. I also tried to include advice that I would have benefitted from learning before I got started. Tl;dr recommendations Research course options. The specific classes you choose may determine your availability for extracurricular leadership (including building an EA group). Ask for help organizing. Two ways to find co-organizers are by posting on class pages/groupchats, and searching for classmates on LinkedIn who follow EA pages. Publicize your group frequently at the very beginning of the school year, when students are most open to joining new clubs. Look for university-wide distribution channels like residential college emails lists where possible. Feel free to repurpose material from&nbsp; this doc with all of the emails Princeton EA sent last year, and the logistics, presentations, and facilitator prep we used for our intro to EA discussion program. Encourage classmates interested in summer internships with impactful nonprofits to seek funding from the university for volunteer work, then post on platforms like the EA Forum or&nbsp; EA Anywhere Slack about seeking summer volunteer opportunities. Act with integrity. Community building success is relational, gradual, and downstream of mutual trust and respect. Other resources The Center for Effective Altruism Organizer Support Program and&nbsp; Groups Resource Center Network for EA Support and Training (NEST) , a&nbsp; post about funding and mentorship, and a partnership with Scott Alexander for&nbsp; university EA groups to host ACX meetups Additional resources for discussions and social events My email if you have any questions (sa9156[at] princeton.edu ) Making school more manageable My personal experience has been that employers aren’t too concerned with the specific classes students take. In my view, employers may care about GPA and major (though for most roles major doesn’t matter much), your work experience, and your extracurricular leadership. I’m confident that high-impact organizations&nbsp; are excited when students organize impactful clubs successfully; group organizing is important, and doing it well is a legible indicator of a student’s aptitudes and mission-alignment. All else equal, I suspect that many high-impact orgs would prefer to hire someone who did a great job organizing their school’s EA group and got a 3.7 GPA as a music major than someone who got a 3.8 in quantum physics and had no EA engagement. I recommend using&nbsp; Ratemyprofessors.com and noting the “difficulty” rating for professors with a large sample of ratings (though the “quality” rating is important for your own happiness!) Even better if you can read through the qualitative reviews to get a sense of a class’ time commitment. You could use a prompt like the following on Claude:&nbsp; Please look up all of the professors on this fall course list on RateMyProfessors and organize them by difficulty and quality ratings. You could also post Fizz asking if upperclassmen have taken certain classes and what the time commitment was like. In my experience, the classes that take the most time are those that assign lots of readings. I think speed-reading the materials and asking an LLM a few questions to confirm you understand the key points can save a considerable amount of time. [2] I also recommend asking upperclassmen for their advice about your major/interests. E.g: You may be able to switch your grading for classes to pass-fail until the last week or two of the semester. This is good to know from the outset so that you can plan around this opportunity. You may be able to take student-taught classes for credit. This can be a great experience, and require considerably less work than professor-taught classes. With a fixed budget of hours, you may find that going to office hours or TA review sessions for 1:1 mentorship better meets your goals than going to lecture classes (particularly if attendance/participation isn’t graded). My view is that you can lean into what you find interesting. For the classes you’re enjoying, you should take every opportunity to learn. But for a brutal calculus requirement or an organic chemistry gen-ed, you may prefer to spend less time on school and instead do the things that make you happy. I think it is valid to choose happiness. [3] Asking for help organizing Getting help organizing your group is one of the highest leverage ways to take pressure off yourself, make organizing more fun, and enable your group to have more impact. The first step to getting help is reaching out to others. If you are starting a brand new group or reviving a group that was largely inactive the previous year, you can post in university or class-wide groupchats (Instagram, WhatsApp, Facebook, Slack etc), saying you’re excited to start a club and you’d love to connect with other students who are interested in EA or doing good broadly about working together to launch it.&nbsp;&nbsp; Another place to look for co-organizers is on LinkedIn for users who have joined EA groups (e.g,&nbsp; 80,000 Hours ), or for anyone from your school who follow EA-related public figures.&nbsp; To do the latter, search the name of your school in the search bar, then click “People”, then click “all filters”. Then scroll down to “followers of” and type in EA influencers (I recommend starting with&nbsp; Rutger Bregman , since he has the largest LinkedIn presence.)&nbsp; Then when you’ve found other current students at your university, you can send them a friendly message (either on LinkedIn, or through your university email platform) asking if they’re interested in hopping on a brief call to help start the club! If you’re at a school that had a group last year but you are the only organizer for this year, I recommend reaching out individually to group members who could be great organizers! People love getting messages that make them feel valued, and they’ll probably be excited about the potential impact of organizing too. [4] If you’re at a school with a well-established group and other co-organizers already, asking for help might mean working with your co-organizers to scope out specific functions or projects for other group members to own. These can include: Core organizers to run learning fellowships, support career planning, conference and internship applications. A communications specialist to advertise the group on social media accounts, draft emails, manage tabling at and outside the club fairs, etc. A fun activity organizer&nbsp; to set up game nights, retreats and other group bonding. An events chair to set up guest speakers talks, and cross-club coordination for joint events with related student groups like AI alignment, vegan society, climate groups and other service clubs. A treasurer to apply for group funding from the university and help group members navigate the process of securing university funding for volunteer internships with impactful organizations. Here is a sample list of university funding. A few schools (Duke, Stanford, MIT, Princeton, Harvard, UChicago, Dartmouth, Cornell, Berkeley and Tufts) have particularly easy processes for seeking summer funding. A special projects lead to organize&nbsp; impactful actions that the group can do, e.g, meeting with your school’s administration about starting high-impact university-affiliated institutes like&nbsp; SERI , advocating for a for-credit class to be taught on EA ideas (e.g,&nbsp; Practical Ethics ), making a book like&nbsp; 80k’s career guide or&nbsp; Doing Good Better the school-sponsored summer “pre-read”. Starting the year with a plan, and hitting the ground running! I recommend reading&nbsp; this post on the importance of the start of the school year. In short, students (particularly freshmen) are much more open to joining new clubs at the start of fall than any other time of year. This makes it the best time to promote your group! I'd also recommend looking into whether your school offers platforms where clubs can reach a large proportion of the student body (e.g, listservs, residential colleges or department mail forwarding) who have opted into receiving messages from student groups. [5] You and your co-organizers may also benefit from mapping out a calendar of monthly goals. Below is the rough plan we have in mind for Princeton EA: Indicators of success University EA groups aim to help students discover and pursue ideas about helping others effectively. One of the main ways students can improve the world is through their careers, however it can be challenging to measure how your group is doing while members are still in school. As intermediary goals, you might track: Email list signups. Attendance at weekly meetings and social events. Applications, and ultimately attendees, at conferences and retreats. Applications, and ultimately recipients, of career advice. Individuals applying and starting at impactful summer internships and full time jobs. Graduates who stay engaged with EA (e.g, respond to emails you send about opportunities for pursuing impactful work). Engaged organizers. Succession (at least 2-3 lead organizers confirmed for the following year). The group’s discussion quality and inclusiveness. Ideally: Group members feel comfortable asking questions when they don’t understand something, think for themselves, reflect on what they believe, and apply the EA mindset to the broader world. Group members with different goals or causal focuses feel like they belong. There are a mix of people who feel bought into “hardcore EA” and people still coming around to EA. Organizers and other group members are accepting of those who are still learning, and those who don’t bite every bullet. Every member, particularly the group leaders, acts with integrity and kindness. Organizers are the types of people who their peers want to be around, and they show that the EA group is inclusive, ambitious, truthful and open-minded. Closing thoughts on organizing Students are unusually open-minded. Most don’t have a mortgage or other sunk costs preventing them from pursuing impactful work. (I think) EA ideas are intrinsically compelling and speak for themselves. By merely making someone aware of EA ideas, you create the opportunity for these ideas to change their life. If you cause someone to pursue an impactful career who would not have otherwise, you may have doubled your lifetime impact. I don’t think it matters&nbsp; who&nbsp; does good. I think people already in important roles -- or who have a lot of EA context -- tend to overestimate their own long term impact relative to others who aren’t as far along yet. Everyone starts somewhere. I think it’s hard to predict where impact will come from, and that anyone who pursues impactful work over the long term has the potential to change the world. There is an enormous amount of money coming into EA, and there has never been a greater need for talent to enable this funding to best help others. I believe that the most successful university EA groups are those that develop students’ personal values and care for doing good effectively. [6] &nbsp;Towards this goal, I think organizers can: 1) Help students connect with the broader EA community (via in-person events and career opportunities) to build lasting social connections.&nbsp; 2) Make EA accessible. EA values will feel right to some and not others; I recommend giving everyone the opportunity to engage with these ideas, then building deeper relationships with the people who show the most excitement. 3) Act with integrity. Most people associate ideas with those who share them, and the decency and virtue group leaders demonstrate can have an outsized impression on the group’s members and long-term reputation. ^ &nbsp;In college, I didn’t even think to start an EA group despite being excited about EA ideas and attending a school that didn’t have a group. ^ It’s against certain class policies to have AI summarize readings for you, but not usually against the policy to check your understanding of readings with AI by asking it questions. Doing so can help you feel confident in the materials after just one pass. ^ You can also pursue self-directed learning (e.g, through your EA group, using Claude as a tutor, via Youtube or podcasts, work experience, etc), which for me has been more practical and enjoyable than what I learn in most classes.&nbsp; ^ Anecdotally, I reached out to 12 Princeton EA members about spending 2 hours per week per cohort facilitating our summer fellowship. 9 of them said yes, including a few who are organizing multiple cohorts. ^ At Princeton, learning about&nbsp; HoagieMail (which clubs use to message most undergraduates) was the single biggest game-changer for our reach. ^ Some students may drop out to do full time impactful work. Some students may get EA jobs straight after graduating college. But for the most part, the impact of university EA groups will come from people who are passionate about EA doing high-impact work further along in their career. Many professionals who were a part of their university EA groups found their way to an impactful job years after college. Even among those who start doing impactful work during or after college, they’ll likely have most of their impact later in their career when they have more responsibility and experience. Discuss

## [A shot-scraper-style JSON API on Bun 1.4's new Bun.WebView](https://simonwillison.net/2026/Aug/20/bun-webview-json-api/)
*Simon Willison's Blog* | 20/08/2026 | Score: 0.80
Tags: research_paper, api_update

> <p><strong>Research:</strong> <a href="https://github.com/simonw/research/tree/main/bun-webview-json-api#readme">A shot-scraper-style JSON API on Bun 1.4's new Bun.WebView</a></p> <p>Today saw the long awaited <a href="https://bun.com/blog/bun-v1.4">release of Bun 1.4</a>, the first stable version since the infamous Rust rewrite <a href="https://simonwillison.net/2026/Jul/8/rewriting-bun-in-rust/">a few months ago</a>.</p> <p>Interestingly, the Rust rewrite was downplayed in the release notes, which introduced a bewildering array of new features and claimed 2,900 additional bug fixes:</p> <blockquote> <p>Bun 1.4 adds +1,517 tests from the Node.js test suite - our biggest jump in Node.js compatibility since Bun 1.0. Bun v1.4 also fixes over 2,900 issues. It reduces idle CPU usage by 5x, reduces memory usage by up to 35%, and starts 50% faster on Linux. It adds <a href="https://bun.com/blog/bun-v1.4#bun-image"><code>Bun.Image</code></a>, <a href="https://bun.com/blog/bun-v1.4#bun-webview"><code>Bun.WebView</code></a>, <a href="https://bun.com/blog/bun-v1.4#bun-markdown"><code>Bun.markdown</code></a>, <a href="https://bun.com/blog/bun-v1.4#bun-cron"><code>Bun.cron()</code></a>, <a href="https://bun.com/blog/bun-v1.4#bun-terminal"><code>Bun.Terminal</code></a>, <a href="https://bun.com/blog/bun-v1.4#bun-run-parallel"><code>bun run --parallel</code></a>, <a href="https://bun.com/blog/bun-v1.4#bun-test-parallel"><code>bun test --parallel</code></a>, <a href="https://bun.com/blog/bun-v1.4#bun-audit-fix"><code>bun audit fix</code></a>, <a href="https://bun.com/blog/bun-v1.4#bun-dedupe"><code>bun dedupe</code></a>, and <a href="https://bun.com/blog/bun-v1.4#bun-prune"><code>bun prune</code></a>. And it rewrites Bun from Zig to Rust.</p> </blockquote> <p>Of these the one that most caught my eye was <code>Bun.WebView</code>, which adds first class support for browser automation to Bun core using either macOS WebKit or control of a local Chromium process via the Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP).</p> <p>I had Claude Code for web build a prototype of a web API providing the ability to load a web page and then execute JavaScript against it, inspired by my <a href="https://shot-scraper.datasette.io/en/stable/javascript.html">shot-scraper javascript</a> CLI tool - partly to see how much RAM would be needed by such a service.</p> <p>Here's <a href="https://github.com/simonw/research/blob/main/bun-webview-json-api/server.ts">that TypeScript server implementation</a>, which appears to need a 192MB-256MB container to run a full Chrome against complex web pages - tested using cgroups.</p> <p>Tags: <a href="https://simonwillison.net/tags/browsers">browsers</a>, <a href="https://simonwillison.net/tags/javascript">javascript</a>, <a href="https://simonwillison.net/tags/ai">ai</a>, <a href="https://simonwillison.net/tags/rust">rust</a>, <a href="https://simonwillison.net/tags/typescript">typescript</a>, <a href="https://simonwillison.net/tags/generative-ai">generative-ai</a>, <a href="https://simonwillison.net/tags/llms">llms</a>, <a href="https://simonwillison.net/tags/coding-agents">coding-agents</a>, <a href="https://simonwillison.net/tags/bun">bun</a></p>
